query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A precipitation‐heat treatment that induces a controlled formation of nanoscale, coherent Ni3Ti-type precipitates in a high-entropy alloy where titanium and nickel are the primary constituents will improve the elevated-temperature yield strength compared to the as-cast single‐phase alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic high-entropy matrix with titanium and nickel as the dominant elements (e.g., Ti35, Ni35, plus minor additions such as Nb10, Mo10, and Cr10 in at.% to satisfy the 5–35 at% rule) that forms a single-phase solid solution when as-cast.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled aging (precipitation) heat treatment (for instance, holding at ~800 °C for a specified time) to induce the nucleation and growth of coherent Ni3Ti-type intermetallic precipitates within the matrix.
generation.conditions: Heat treatment should be performed in an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation, with temperatures in the range of 750–850 °C and time tuned to yield a fine, uniform dispersion of precipitates, while mechanical properties are evaluated at elevated temperatures (e.g., 700–1200 °C).
generation.structural_mediator: The nanoscale, coherent Ni3Ti-type (or similar) precipitates that form within the predominantly Ti-Ni matrix.
generation.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening: The finely dispersed, coherent precipitates act as obstacles against dislocation motion at high temperatures, thereby increasing the yield strength and delaying the onset of plastic deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The heat-treated alloy will show a measurable increase in elevated-temperature yield strength (potentially on the order of 10–30% higher) relative to the untreated, homogeneous as-cast alloy, while maintaining adequate ductility.
generation.baseline: The as-cast single-phase Ti-Ni primary high-entropy alloy without the precipitation heat treatment.
generation.boundary: Alloy composition must conform to the HEA definition (each element between 5 and 35 at%), and the improved properties are expected in the elevated-temperature range (approximately 700–1200 °C); outcomes outside these temperature ranges or with deviating compositions are not covered by this hypothesis.
generation.uncertainty: The exact precipitate phase, optimal heat-treatment temperature/time, and magnitude of improvement (whether near the predicted 10–30% gain) require experimental calibration. It is also uncertain how the presence of minor elements (Nb, Mo, Cr) may affect both precipitation kinetics and high-temperature deformation behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the targeted Ti-Ni primary high-entropy alloy with the same overall composition (e.g., Ti35, Ni35, Nb10, Mo10, Cr10 at.%). Leave one batch in the as-cast state and subject the other batch to the specified aging heat treatment (e.g., 800 °C for an optimized time in an inert atmosphere). Machine identical test specimens from both batches.
measurements: Perform elevated-temperature tensile or compressive tests in the range of 700–1200 °C to determine yield strength and ductility.
Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) or high-resolution scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to confirm the presence, size, and dispersion of nano-scale precipitates in the heat-treated alloy.
Conduct microstructural characterization (e.g., X-ray diffraction) to compare phase constitution of treated and untreated samples.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in elevated-temperature yield strength (e.g., less than a 10% increase when compared to the as-cast state) or if no nanoscale precipitates can be clearly identified in the microstructure, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo. AbstractSingle-phase solid-solution refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) have been receiving significant attention due to their excellent mechanical properties and phase stability at elevated temperatures. Recently, many studies have been reported regarding the precipitation-enhanced alloy design strategy to further improve the mechanical properties of RHEAs at elevated temperatures. In this study, we attempted to develop precipitation-hardened light-weight RHEAs via addition of Ni or Co into Al0.8NbTiV HEA. The added elements were selected due to their smaller atomic radius and larger mixing enthalpy, which is known to stimulate the formation of precipitates. The addition of the Ni or Co leads to the formation of the sigma precipitates with homogeneous distribution. The formation and homogeneous distribution of sigma particles plays a critical role in improvement of yield strength. Furthermore, the Al0.8NbTiVM0.2 (M = Co, Ni) HEAs show excellent specific yield strength compared to single-phase AlNbTiV and NbTiVZr RHEA alloys and conventional Ni-based superalloy (Inconel 718) at elevated temperatures.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory alloys, lightweight, sigma phase, mech
